name: libaco
workload: Pure context-switch microbenchmark (test_aco_benchmark.c) of acosw vs libco coctx_swap, standalone stacks.
claimed_speedup: acosw is 1.72x faster than Tencent libco's coctx_swap; acosw 17.64 ns/op in that branch's run; main README reports ~10.29 ns per switch.
hardware: AWS c5d.large, RHEL-7.5 (exact CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: x86/x86-64 SysV ABI only (Intel386 and AMD64), asymmetric coroutines, one libaco instance per thread, optional copy-stack sharing; must call aco_exit instead of return.
caveats: First-party benchmark; compiler version and CPU model not stated so below tier A. libco comparison lives on a side branch, not master README. Does not compare to Boost.Context. Last commit 2022.
found_via: WebSearch: coroutine library faster than libco Tencent benchmark context switch github C++ coroutine

name: libcopp
workload: Coroutine switch overhead with 1, 1000 and 30000 coroutines (16 KB, 2 MB, 64 KB stacks) in an owent gist comparing libcopp, libco, libgo, goroutine and ucontext.
claimed_speedup: libcopp 77/105/273 ns vs libco (static stack pool) 84/168/450 ns per switch at 1/1000/30000 coroutines (about 1.1x/1.6x/1.65x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Stackful coroutines plus C++20 coroutine support; stack pools; cross-platform (Linux, Windows, macOS, MinGW).
caveats: Benchmark is a 2019 gist by the libcopp author with no hardware, compiler or flags stated; libgo is faster than libcopp in the same table; Boost.Context not in this table. Repo README points to CI benchmark reports I did not open.
found_via: WebSearch: libcopp OR libgo OR libtask coroutine switch benchmark comparison boost.context libco ucontext

name: libgo
workload: Coroutine switch overhead with 1, 1000 and 30000 coroutines in third-party (libcopp author) gist.
claimed_speedup: libgo 30/32/150 ns vs libco (static stack pool) 84/168/450 ns per switch at 1/1000/30000 coroutines (about 2.8x/5.3x/3x, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Go-style scheduler with channels, multithreaded runtime; heavier than a bare context-switch library; uses Boost.Context assembly internally in recent versions.
caveats: Numbers come from a 2019 gist by the competing libcopp author, no hardware or flags; gist notes libgo at that time was an older version and later merged boost.context. libgo's own README compares only to Go. Switching from Boost.Context-based code means this is not a win over Boost.Context itself.
found_via: WebSearch: libcopp OR libgo OR libtask coroutine switch benchmark comparison boost.context libco ucontext

name: minicoro
workload: CPU cycles per context switch, init and uninit of pre-allocated coroutines, Linux x86_64, assembly vs ucontext backend.
claimed_speedup: 9 cycles per context switch (assembly) vs 352 cycles (ucontext) on Linux x86_64; Windows 33 cycles (assembly) vs 69 (fibers).
license: Unlicense OR MIT-0 (public domain or MIT No Attribution)
tradeoffs: Single-header pure C stackful coroutines, assembly backends for x86_64, ARM, RISC-V; ucontext/fibers fallback.
caveats: Baseline is ucontext (not in category list); no comparison to Boost.Context or libco. A third-party issue on ucoro (a minicoro fork) found its switch about 3x slower than Boost.Context at 5.9-6.1 ns round trip, with a return-misprediction cause; upstream minicoro may share it (not verified). Compiler and flags not stated. Public domain: no patent grant.
found_via: WebSearch: stackful coroutine library C++ paper context switch cycles benchmark source code github

name: libseff
workload: OOPSLA 2024 evaluation of effect-handler implementations and concurrency mechanisms (context switch, skynet, http server benchmarks), including libco and cppcoro.
claimed_speedup: Paper reports libseff consistently fastest among effect-handler libraries; numbers versus libco not read (paper PDF blocked).
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6154, Ubuntu 20.04 (from search snippet)
tradeoffs: Effect-handler API (shallow handlers) on asymmetric stackful coroutines, segmented stacks, x86-64 focus; C library with its own API, not a drop-in coroutine library.
caveats: Snippet only: the paper (Effect Handlers for C via Coroutines, OOPSLA 2024) is on blocked hosts, so speedup numbers vs libco are unconfirmed and whether libseff beats libco on switching is unverified; bench/ directory vendors libco and cppcoro as comparison. Mulan PSL v2 is OSI-approved. Low star count.
